Frozen development lessons:
# Frozen development lessons, version 1

These rules were curated with Codex assistance from official training runs.
They contain no task answers and are not updated during held-out evaluation.

## L1: Stop searching after confirming an unavailable external dataset

When execution fails on a network request, inspect the loader and check the
provided data directory once. If the required dataset is neither bundled nor
cached, record the failing request and submit unanswered values with blocker
evidence. Do not repeatedly search the entire filesystem or try alternative
internet endpoints in an offline environment.

20261117T200334263866Z-capsule-4098236-run-A1, artifacts/step-003.stdout.txt
(network failure), step-004.stdout.txt (loader), and step-007.stdout.txt
(repeated broad search). The run eventually exceeded its context bound.

## L2: Execute a notebook once and inspect its structured outputs

For notebook reproduction, save an executed notebook in the results directory,
then render that executed notebook to the requested presentation format. Locate
relevant output cells using the requested metric labels. Print only the needed
output segments. Avoid dumping full notebook source or raw HTML into context,
and avoid executing the whole experiment again merely to read its output.

Source: development capsule-0940461, run
20261117T200757054830Z-capsule-0940461-run-A1, tool steps 003 through 010.
Source dumping and repeated executions preceded a context-limit failure.

## L3: Discover documentation filenames before chaining commands

List the task directory before assuming that README.md exists. Read whichever
instruction file is actually provided and read REPRODUCING.md separately. A
missing optional README should not prevent required instructions from being read.

The first chained command stopped at a missing README; the next inspected the
available files and recovered.

## Scope

These are development-derived workflow heuristics, not verified universal rules.
They may reduce wasted calls without improving final accuracy. Report both cost
and accuracy, and preserve any adverse effects.

53: # For running meta-analyses on proportions (most of the meta analyses in this review).

55: metaDisc <- function(df){
56:   # initialize a dataframe to hold all 40 meta-analytic estimates, CIs, PIs, and number of articles analyzed.
57:   estim <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = 7, nrow = length(df)))
58:   colnames(estim) <- c("b", "lower.random", "upper.random", "lower.predict", "upper.predict", "k", "n")
59:   
60:   # assign the colnames from df to the rownames for estim so that the results line up in the next section of code
61:   rownames(estim) <- colnames(df)
62:   
63:   # initialize lists of lists to hold the results of the 40 meta-analyses
64:   metaList<-list()
65:   
66:   # calculate the meta-analytic estimates, CIs, PIs, and number of articles analyzed for outcomes from prospectively registered studies
67:   for (i in grep("discProAny", colnames(df)):grep("discProTime", colnames(df))){
68:     if (sum(!is.na(df[,i] > 0 ))){
69:       # create temporary dataframe with the NAs removed. This is necessary to align the article author and year with the correct article after running each meta-analysis
70:       dfMeta <- df %>% filter(!is.na(df[,i]))
71:       meta <- meta::metaprop(dfMeta[,i], dfMeta$discProDenom,
72:                           # method for conducting the meta-analytic model (a multi-level regression)
73:                           method="GLMM",
74:                           # method to calculate tau
75:                           method.tau="ML",
76:                           # method to calculate the confidence interval for tau^2 (which we don't report)
77:                           method.tau.ci="J", 
78:                           comb.random=TRUE, 
79:                           prediction=TRUE,
80:                           level.predict=0.95,
81:                           # helpful for meta-analyses of few articles (modifies Student's T-distribution)
82:                           hakn=TRUE
83:       )
84:       # create the study labels for the forest plots
85:       meta$studlab <- paste(dfMeta$author, dfMeta$pubYear)
86:       
87:     metaList[[i]] <- meta #store a list of the meta variable for all 40 meta-analyses to make forest plots later
88:     # All meta-analytic estimates, CIs, and PIs, need to have inv.logit() run on them to reverse the logit() function that is used in the metaprop() function. 
89:     estim[i,] <- c(inv.logit(meta$TE.random), 
90:                    inv.logit(meta$lower.random), 
91:                    inv.logit(meta$upper.random),
92:                    inv.logit(meta$lower.predict),
93:                    inv.logit(meta$upper.predict),
94:                    meta$k,
95:                    sum(meta$data[,2]))
96:         }
97:   }
98:   
99:   # same as above for outcomes from studies with unclear timing of registration.
100:   for (i in grep("discAny", colnames(df)):grep("discTime", colnames(df))){
101:     if (sum(!is.na(df[,i] > 0 ))){
102:       
103:       # create temporary dataframe with the NAs removed

266: # Abstract
267: 
268: **Objectives**. Prospectively registering study plans in a permanent time-stamped and publicly accessible document is becoming more common across disciplines and aims to reduce risk of bias and make risk of bias transparent. Selective reporting persists, however, when researchers deviate from their registered plans without disclosure. This systematic review aimed to estimate the prevalence of undisclosed discrepancies between prospectively registered study plans and their associated publication. We further aimed to identify the research disciplines where these discrepancies have been observed, whether interventions to reduce discrepancies have been conducted, and gaps in the literature.
269: 
270: **Design**. Systematic review and meta-analyses.
271: 
272: **Data sources**. Scopus and Web of Knowledge, published up to 15 December 2019.
273: 
274: **Eligibility criteria**. Articles that included quantitative data about discrepancies between registrations or study protocols and their associated publications.
275: 
276: **Data extraction and synthesis**. Each included article was independently coded by two reviewers using a coding form designed for this review ([osf.io/728ys](https://osf.io/728ys)). We used random-effects meta-analyses to synthesize the results.
277: 
278: **Results**. We reviewed k = `r nrow(df)` articles, which included k = `r nrow(df1)` that reported on primary outcome discrepancies from n = `r sum(df1$discDenom)` studies and, k = `r nrow(df2)` that reported on secondary outcome discrepancies from n = `r sum(df2$discDenom)` studies. Meta-analyses indicated that between `r round(tab["discPro1", "lower.random.2"],2)*100`% to `r round(tab["discPro1", "upper.random.2"],2)*100`% (95% confidence interval) of studies contained at least one primary outcome discrepancy and between `r round(tab["discPro2", "lower.random.2"],2)*100`% to `r round(tab["discPro2", "upper.random.2"],2)*100`% (95% confidence interval) contained at least one secondary outcome discrepancy. Almost all articles assessed clinical literature, and there was considerable heterogeneity. We identified only one article that attempted to correct discrepancies.
279: 
280: **Conclusions**. Many articles did not include information on whether discrepancies were disclosed, which version of a registration they compared publications to, and whether the registration was prospective. Thus, our estimates represent discrepancies broadly, rather than our target of *undisclosed* discrepancies between *prospectively* registered study plans and their associated publications. Discrepancies are common and reduce the trustworthiness of medical research. Interventions to reduce discrepancies could prove valuable.
281: 
282: **Registration**. [osf.io/ktmdg](https://osf.io/ktmdg). Protocol amendments are listed in Supplementary Material A.

286: # Introduction
287: 
288: In 2000, ClinicalTrials.gov and the ISRCTN Registry were launched with several aims, including aiding participant recruitment, facilitating knowledge synthesis, and reducing duplication, publication bias and selective reporting [@zarin2017]. In 2005, the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) made *prospective* registration a condition of consideration for publication [@deangelis2004]. Thousands of journals now claim to follow this policy [@icmje2021]. In parallel, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform established a minimum set of required information for a trial to be considered fully registered, including experimental design elements such as the conditions being studied, intervention, key inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size, primary outcomes, and key secondary outcomes [@sim2006]. While the relatively widespread uptake of clinical trial registration has substantially improved transparency, many trials remain unregistered, are registered after enrollment of participants begins or analyses are complete (i.e., *retrospective* registration), are never published, or publish outcomes discrepant with those in the registration without disclosing the discrepancy [e.g., @chan2017; @scott2015]. Nevertheless, the existence of registries allows researchers to identify and quantify these issues.
289: 
290: In research disciplines other than clinical trials, study registration is becoming more common, but remains far from standard practice [@hardwicke2020e; @hardwicke2021b; @scoggins2023; @thibault2023]. For example, starting around 2011 the field of psychology has increasingly taken the “replication crisis” seriously and many researchers and journals now use registration to reduce bias and make risk of bias transparent. Other disciplines have created dedicated registries, such as PROSPERO for systematic reviews and the American Economic Association RCT Trial Registry.
291: 
292: In this manuscript, we systematically reviewed articles that quantify the prevalence of discrepancies between registrations or study protocols and their associated publications (e.g., in primary outcome measures). Our analysis extended beyond the three systematic reviews already published on this topic in several ways [@li2018; @dwan2013a; @jones2015]. First, registration has expanded beyond clinical trials; we included all research disciplines and used key word searches for registries including the Open Science Framework, the American Economic Association RCT Trial Registry, and PROSPERO. Second, we extracted more fine-grained information about a wide range of discrepancies (e.g., outcomes, analysis, sample size), as well as which version of the registration was surveyed and whether discrepancies were disclosed (we believe disclosed discrepancies present little reason for concern). Third, our review included over twice as many studies as previous systematic reviews on this topic, provides meta-analytic estimates, and used meta-regression and additional analyses to attempt to identify predictors of discrepancies.
